item.title: More and Better Jobs Key to Putting Poverty Reduction Back on Track
item.description: Global progress on reducing extreme poverty has come to a standstill, and the world is at risk of falling further behind unless more and better jobs are created, according to the World Bank Group’s new Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2026. Without stronger per capita growth, the number of people in extreme poverty is projected to be higher in 2030 than it is today.
item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON, October 26, 2026—Global progress on reducing extreme poverty has come to a standstill, and the world is at risk of falling further behind unless more and better jobs are created, according to the World Bank Group’s new Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2026. Without stronger per capita growth, the number of people in extreme poverty is projected to be higher in 2030 than it is today.

In 2026, about 811 million people — one in ten globally — live on less than $3.00 per person per day, a rate that has essentially not changed since the pandemic. To bring extreme poverty down to 3% by 2050, per capita economic growth would need to average around 4% per year — twice the rate achieved over the last 25 years.

“In countries where poverty is the highest, slow growth has held back job creation and limited opportunities for millions of people,” said Pablo Saavedra, World Bank Group Vice President for Prosperity. “We need to accelerate growth and enable the creation of more and better jobs as a key pathway out of poverty.”

The report notes that extreme poverty remains concentrated: More than half of the world's extremely poor live in just nine economies, and by 2030 an estimated 87% are projected to live in Sub-Saharan Africa or in fragile and conflict-affected situations.

Nearly half the global population — 3.7 billion people — still lives on less than $8.30/day, a number that has remained stagnant since 1990. The World Bank uses international poverty lines to track deprivation across different income contexts. The $3.00/day line measures extreme poverty and is based on the poverty standards used in low-income countries; the $8.30/day poverty line is the standard for upper-middle-income countries.

Poverty reduction requires both more and better jobs. The report identifies two mutually reinforcing priorities:

  • Closing employment gaps: Raising employment rates in poor households to 75% among working-age adults — which could be attained by closing the gender gap in employment rates — would reduce global extreme poverty by roughly one-fifth.
  • Closing earning gaps: Poor workers are concentrated in low-return activities such as smallholder farming and have lower education levels. Raising their education to the average attained by people above the extreme poverty line would increase predicted earnings by around 40% and cut extreme poverty nearly in half. Moving them into wage work or out of agriculture would cut poverty by about one-fifth.

The priorities differ across countries, but the goal is the same: Help farmers and small businesses earn more, create opportunities for better jobs, and bring more women into the workforce. More and better jobs are not only a path out of poverty. They are the foundation for economic security and a growing middle class.

“Even under challenging circumstances, progress is possible for improving lives and moving more people out of poverty,” said Michael Kremer, World Bank Group Chief Economist and Senior Vice President for Development Economics. “This report provides the framework for understanding the challenges and identifying the primary approaches for reducing poverty.”

item.title: World Bank Group Launches First Digital Strategy to Expand Access and Create Jobs
item.description: The World Bank Group today launched its first digital strategy, bringing together its public and private sector capabilities to help developing countries expand affordable digital access, improve services, and create jobs.
item.content:encoded:
SEOUL, October 20, 2026— The World Bank Group today launched its first digital strategy, bringing together its public and private sector capabilities to help developing countries expand affordable digital access, improve services, and create jobs.

The strategy addresses four priorities: expanding connectivity; making devices and data more affordable; strengthening digital services and skills; and helping countries build the foundations to benefit from artificial intelligence.

“Digital technology can help countries create jobs and make scarce resources go further. Realizing that potential requires a comprehensive approach—from reliable connectivity and affordable devices to digital skills and useful services,” said World Bank Group President Ajay Banga. “Our first digital strategy brings these pieces together, helping countries build the foundations to benefit from today’s digital tools and the promise of small AI—AI for the people.”

The launch comes as developing countries face twin challenges: constrained resources and a growing need for jobs. Over the next 10 to 15 years, 1.2 billion young people will reach working age in developing countries, while their economies are projected to create about 420 million jobs.

Digital technology can support job creation across the World Bank Group’s five priority sectors: infrastructure and energy, agribusiness, health care, tourism, and value-added manufacturing. It can help businesses reach customers, improve productivity, and access finance, while reducing the cost of delivering public services.

Yet substantial barriers remain. Over 2 billion people were offline globally in 2025. Only 23 percent of people in low-income countries used the internet, compared with 94 percent in high-income countries. Many people live within network coverage but cannot afford a smartphone or data, lack digital skills, or have limited access to services relevant to their needs.

The strategy sets out four areas of action:

  • Expand reliable connectivity. The World Bank Group will help countries address gaps across the network, from international cables and national connections to the networks serving homes, businesses, schools, and clinics. Its approach includes supporting shared infrastructure, encouraging competition, and using public finance and guarantees to help attract private investment into underserved markets. Where electricity and connectivity are both missing, the strategy supports planning them together.
  • Make devices and data more affordable. The strategy supports efforts to lower the cost of entry-level smartphones and broadband services that increase the cost of staying connected. Partnerships with manufacturers, mobile operators, financial institutions, and refurbishment businesses can help lower prices and expand responsible options for paying over time.
  • Expand digital services and skills. The World Bank Group will support reliable systems for digital identification, payments, and secure information-sharing that make public and private services easier to access. It will also help countries strengthen digital literacy and training linked to employment, enabling more people and small businesses to use technology safely and productively.
  • Build readiness for AI. The strategy will help countries strengthen connectivity, access computing resources, develop usable local data, and build skills. It emphasizes practical applications of “small AI”—tools adapted to specific tasks and local conditions, such as helping farmers identify crop disease, supporting health workers, or helping businesses manage inventory.

Safeguards—from privacy to cybersecurity and fraud protection—run across all four priorities.

The strategy brings together the World Bank Group’s financing, policy advice, private investment, and guarantees around country priorities. It also provides a basis for working with governments, technology companies, development partners, and philanthropy to extend digital opportunities to more people and businesses. Its aim is to help countries turn digital access into higher productivity, better services, and more opportunities to earn a living.

Complementing the strategy’s AI readiness and adaptation priority, the World Bank Group also announced the AI Infrastructure and Readiness Initiative. This is a new effort to help governments in emerging markets access affordable compute capacity—and put small AI to productive use—through shared, pay-as-you-go GPU infrastructure (specialized computing power used to develop and run AI applications), offering a practical alternative to standalone national data centers. The initiative will have an initial focus on Africa and Latin America, with knowledge partners including Cassava Technologies and NVIDIA.

item.title: UAE Signs Agreement to Host 2029 World Bank Group and IMF Annual Meetings in Abu Dhabi
item.description: UAE Signs Agreement to Host 2029 World Bank Group and IMF Annual Meetings in Abu Dhabi
item.content:encoded:
BANGKOK, October 18, 2026—The United Arab Emirates has signed the agreement to host the 2029 Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group (WBG) and International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Abu Dhabi.

Signed at the conclusion of the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group in Bangkok, Thailand, the agreement reflects growing international confidence in the UAE’s economic and financial ecosystem. It also reinforces the country’s position as a global financial hub and strategic partner in supporting the stability of the international economic system and shaping its future direction.

The agreement was signed by H.E. Mohamed bin Hadi Al Hussaini, Minister of State for Financial Affairs, and H.E. Khaled Mohamed Balama, Governor of the Central Bank of the UAE and the UAE Governor to the International Monetary Fund.

Representing the two international institutions, Ajay Banga, President of the World Bank Group, and Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund, also signed the agreement in the presence of a number of senior officials.

Commenting on the occasion, H.E. Mohamed bin Hadi Al Hussaini, Minister of State for Financial Affairs, said the signing of the agreement to host the 2029 Annual Meetings translates the UAE leadership’s vision into action by advancing the resilience and competitiveness of the country’s economic model, expanding international partnerships and promoting multilateral cooperation.

“The signing of the agreement marks a significant milestone, reflecting the international community’s enduring confidence in the UAE’s readiness, the efficiency of its infrastructure and financial system, and its ability to host major international events of strategic importance,” he said

“By hosting this landmark gathering, the UAE is committed to providing a global platform that brings together financial sector leaders and decision-makers from around the world to explore ways of advancing financial and monetary stability and developing mechanisms for development finance.”

Al Hussaini added that the UAE’s selection to host these global meetings builds on the country’s successful track record in hosting major economic events and its direct role in supporting sustainable development and digital transformation.

He reaffirmed that the UAE would continue coordinating and cooperating with the IMF and the World Bank Group to put in place all the facilities and organizational capabilities required to ensure the success of the 2029 Annual Meetings in Abu Dhabi.

This, he said, would help deliver substantive outcomes that advance international economic cooperation, serve the aspirations of people and support the growth of emerging and advanced economies alike.

For his part, H.E. Khaled Mohamed Balama, Governor of the Central Bank of the UAE and the UAE Governor to the International Monetary Fund, said: “Abu Dhabi’s hosting of the 2029 Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund reflects the UAE leadership’s efforts to reinforce the country’s global leadership and the competitiveness of its financial system on the international stage, while reaffirming the UAE’s position as a global hub for shaping the future of the international financial system.

“This selection is a testament to international confidence in the strength of the UAE’s financial and banking sector and the efficiency of the financial, regulatory and monetary infrastructure overseen by the Central Bank, further enhancing the UAE’s ability to play a pivotal role in advancing the multilateral financial agenda.”

He added: “Through this strategic hosting, the Central Bank of the UAE looks forward to leading international efforts to advance global financial and monetary stability, accelerate secure digital innovation and drive the transition towards sustainable finance.

“We are committed to providing a leading global platform that brings together central bank leaders, decision-makers and international financial institutions to discuss practical and innovative solutions that enhance the resilience of the global economy in the face of change and support inclusive and sustainable growth.”

Through this hosting, the Central Bank of the UAE will bring the UAE’s expertise in financial stability, financial infrastructure development and innovation in digital financial services to the global discussion, reinforcing its role as a key partner in designing practical solutions to address global economic challenges and support pathways towards inclusive and sustainable growth.

Ajay Banga, President of the World Bank Group, said: “The UAE has built institutions and infrastructure with a spirit of bold ambition and partnership, cementing its role as a global hub for economic dialogue. Abu Dhabi is a fitting host for the Annual Meetings where our focus is on development impact, and delivering jobs, growth, and financing at scale.”

For her part, Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), said: “I am delighted that the United Arab Emirates will host the IMF membership at our Annual Meetings in 2029. The UAE has become an important hub for ideas, finance, innovation, and international cooperation. We look forward to coming together there in 2029 to discuss the challenges and opportunities ahead and help shape a better future.”

H.E. Ahmed Jasim Al Zaabi, Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Department of Economic Development (ADDED), said: “Hosting the 2029 Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund in Abu Dhabi is a significant milestone for the UAE and reflects the international community’s confidence in Abu Dhabi as a trusted centre for global economic and financial dialogue.

“Abu Dhabi brings together the institutional strength, regulatory certainty and long-term investment capacity needed to support sustainable economic growth. Our focus is on fostering an environment where capital can move with confidence, businesses can grow with speed and certainty, and investment translates into lasting economic value.

“As we prepare to welcome the world’s economic and financial leaders in 2029, we look forward to contributing to the global conversation on the future of growth, investment and international economic cooperation.”

Hosting the 2029 Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group and IMF in Abu Dhabi will provide an important platform for international economic cooperation and dialogue.

The meetings are set to bring together finance ministers, central bank governors, policymakers and economic experts, private sector representatives, civil society, media, and academics from 191 countries to examine the challenges and opportunities facing the global economy, the outlook for growth and financial stability, and future policies capable of supporting inclusive and sustainable development.

The formal signing builds on the UAE’s longstanding partnership with the IMF and the World Bank Group, and marks the country’s second time hosting the Annual Meetings, following Dubai in 2003. Hosting the Meetings in Abu Dhabi will provide an opportunity to advance international cooperation and multilateral dialogue on the key challenges facing the global economy.

It will also cement Abu Dhabi’s role as a global center for economic decision-making and a platform for multilateral financial dialogue..

item.title: Remarks by World Bank Group President Ajay Banga at the 2026 Annual Meetings Plenary
item.description: In the months before I joined the World Bank Group in June 2023, three truths emerged clearly from conversations with shareholders, clients, private sector leaders, philanthropies, and others.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning.

Let me begin by thanking the Prime Minister and the people of Thailand for your generous hospitality. Deputy Prime Minister, Governor—thank you for the care and hard work you and your teams have put into these Meetings. And to our Chair, thank you for your leadership. It is a pleasure to be here with all of you.

In the months before I joined the World Bank Group in June 2023, three truths emerged clearly from conversations with shareholders, clients, private sector leaders, philanthropies, and others.

The challenges were great. Resources were limited. And the World Bank Group needed to face the wind.

Three years later, the wind has not eased. Conflicts persist. Fiscal space is tighter. Debt burdens have risen. And cost of essentials—from energy to fertilizer—remains high.

Meanwhile, a demographic transformation is unfolding.

Over the next 10 to 15 years, 1.2 billion young people will arrive at a job market projected to offer only about 400 million jobs.

This generation will shape the next century. The choices we make today will help determine how.

Those are the twin challenges we have been working to address:

Making scarce resources go further… while helping countries create jobs at scale.

They must be addressed together.

Over the past three years, I have used these Annual Meetings to lay out the work we were undertaking, changes we were making, and the ambition behind them.

This year, I want to focus on our progress—and where it is taking us.

The future of development will depend on bringing public finance, private investment, philanthropy, and technology together around what each country needs.

The partnership—and mix—should evolve as countries do.

Where needs and risks are greatest, public and concessional finance will remain essential. As countries grow stronger, private investment and access to markets should play a larger role. And to be clear success arrives when we are no longer needed by a country.

We have seen that journey. Thirty-five countries have moved from IDA to IBRD. Twenty-three are now IDA donors themselves. That is exactly what we want, and our strategy is built around what makes that progress possible.

It began with changing the World Bank Group itself.

We cut project preparation from 19 months to nine. Replaced 153 scorecard measures with 22 focused on impact. Increased pay-for-results financing from about one-third to half. Brought our public and private sector teams together around country-led strategies. And reengineered our balance sheet—creating more than $100 billion in additional IBRD lending capacity over a decade.

We are also making it easier for MDBs to work together.

The number of projects on our digital co-financing platform has tripled in two years to about 250 projects, seeking $138 billion in financing. We are cutting duplication by relying on each other’s work with the Asian Development Bank, Inter-American Development Bank and EBRD—and expanding that model.

Taken together, these changes give us greater capacity.

Our jobs strategy gives it direction.

The Jobs Council drew on experience across countries and sectors to identify policies and programs that create more and better jobs. The strategy that emerged rests on three pillars.

First, physical and human infrastructure. Employers need electricity, water, transport, and digital connections. People need health, education, and skills. Last year, we committed $40 billion—nearly one-third of our financing—to these foundations.

Second, regulatory and policy certainty. Businesses of every size depend on strong institutions, good governance, and clear rules—from simpler permits to predictable land laws. Last year, 30 percent of our public sector financing supported policy and institutional reform.

Third, scale. Even with strong foundations and clear rules, some risks still hold investment back. The Private Sector Investment Lab helped us focus on those barriers—from currency risk to access to finance—and strengthen the tools to address them: guarantees, equity, and local currency financing.

That is how we bring more private capital into development.

The results are beginning to show.

In FY22—the year before our workplan began—we mobilized roughly $35 billion in private capital. Last year: $112 billion. A threefold increase.

Alongside our own financing, total financing exceeded $230 billion.

Gains are being felt across the spectrum. Mobilization nearly tripled in lower-middle-income countries, quadrupled in upper-middle-income countries, and more than doubled across Africa.

Our challenge is that in low-income countries, where attracting commercial capital remains hardest, mobilization held flat. The path to the poorest and most fragile economies runs through their small businesses—often growing where larger companies have yet to take root. Our new MSME strategy aims to reach where opportunity is hardest to come by.

Participation is broadening too.

Last year, we mobilized capital from investors in 110 countries. The United States, United Kingdom, and India led the way. But investors also came from Romania, Chile, Poland, and Brazil.

More countries are attracting investment. More are supplying it.

Across it all, nearly 55 percent of our financing and the private capital we mobilized went to infrastructure and energy, agribusiness, health, tourism, and value-added manufacturing—sectors that we are focused on to create jobs.

And total World Bank Group climate co-benefits reached $96 billion—$48 billion came from private capital. $96 billion. One institution. One year.

But financing is only the beginning.

The real value is bringing that capacity together around what each country is trying to achieve. That is why country strategies and compacts matter. Roadmaps built around a country’s ambitions, the results we are trying to achieve together, and the investments and reforms required to get there.

The roadmap is bespoke. The discipline is consistent.

We show up bringing public and private sector capabilities together from the start. We use IDA and our balance sheet where public and concessional resources are needed, align with philanthropic and operational partners, and mobilize private capital where markets can support it.

Technology amplifies that work.

“Big AI” requires computing power, energy, data, specialized skills, and capital that put frontier models beyond many developing countries’ immediate reach.

But practical, or “small,” AI can help a farmer improve yields, a teacher tailor instruction, a health worker make better-informed decisions, or an entrepreneur reach new customers. So we are helping countries build the electricity, connectivity, device access, and safeguards to put those tools to work.

Skills are part of the package—connecting education and training more closely to the jobs and industries countries are building.

So are small businesses. Our MSME strategy, launched earlier this week, is designed to make firms more visible, connected, enabled, and funded—using digital records to improve access to finance, link smaller businesses to larger buyers and markets, and simplify the rules that allow them to grow.

Critically important, in fragile and conflict-affected settings, where conditions do not yet support larger companies, small businesses play an outsized role in creating jobs and laying the foundations for stability.

Embedded across everything we do—building resilient infrastructure and stronger institutions so progress lasts.

That is what we refer to as smart development.

Our method is producing results.

Start with energy.

Through Mission 300, our ambition with the African Development Bank is to bring electricity to 300 million people in Africa by 2030.

So far, 59 million have gained access. And the pace has accelerated—from 12 million in FY24, to 18 million in FY25, to 29 million last year.

But access is only part of the challenge. Homes, mines, factories, farms, and growing cities need reliable, affordable baseload power.

Our approach is balanced by design—a full mix of renewables, hydro, gas where appropriate, nuclear where it makes sense, transmission, grids, and storage. That includes supporting nuclear retrofits with the IAEA—the first such work in 50 years.

On water, our ambition with partners is to improve water security for up to one billion people by 2030, with the World Bank Group committed to 400 million. Twenty country compacts give us a path to reach 150 million people with clean water. Twenty more compacts are on the horizon.

In agriculture, private, philanthropic, and operational partners are working to help 300 million smallholder farmers move from subsistence to surplus by 2030, with the World Bank Group committed to 200 million. We built a pipeline to support 82 million farmers in AgriConnect’s first full year and are doing the spade work for the next 118 million.

Through HealthWorks—supported by the Japanese government—our ambition is to reach 1.5 billion people with quality, affordable health services by 2030. Roughly 600 million have already been reached. The same model is showing up in newer areas.

In critical minerals, we plan to multiply our business five times in five years. This week, we launched our first country compacts with MDB partners—to build local industries and keep more jobs and value at home. We’ve identified 20 countries who we could partner with on this work.

In economic corridors, we launched 52 new projects last year—up from 20 three years earlier. With partners like the European Commission’s Global Gateway, Italy's Mattei Plan, and the United States' DFC, we are bringing infrastructure and investment together.

The infrastructure connects places. The opportunity grows along the way.

In Lobito, a route principally for minerals is increasingly carrying farmers’ crops to markets—and helping towns and cities grow.

Different sectors. Different countries. Different solutions.

Same objective: advance development and generate jobs.

The next phase is execution at scale.

That means meeting private-sector clients where they invest and make decisions.

We are expanding our presence in New York, Frankfurt, Milan, and Tokyo—to originate opportunities, solve problems faster, and build stronger pipelines.

But stronger pipelines are only part of the answer.

Development finance has always faced a basic constraint: a dollar can only be in one place at a time. Finance a power project, and that capital is fixed for decades—unavailable for the next water system, rail corridor, or clinic countries need.

Meanwhile, pension funds, insurers, and sovereign wealth funds manage enormous pools of long-term capital looking for long-term investments.

We are making the introduction.

Six multilateral development banks are creating common ways to assess, document, package, and transfer investments—so a project we help finance today can be held by another investor tomorrow, freeing our capital for the next one.

Repeated across institutions and markets, that begins to create something much bigger: an emerging-market development asset class. If we get this right, the size of our balance sheet no longer defines the scale of our ambition—and we will bend the curve of development forever.

Let me end where this institution began.

In 1944, with the world still at war, delegates from forty-four nations gathered in the mountains of New Hampshire.

They had every reason to turn inward. Instead, they made a wager: that rebuilding one nation could strengthen others, and recovery was a shared responsibility.

They did not build a monument to charity. They built a Bank and a Fund.

They understood something we must never forget: prosperity is not a prize one nation wins from another. It is a fire that warms every house within reach.

As countries’ needs changed, this institution changed with them—developing new ways to finance development and support private enterprise.

Building knowledge over decades of work.

Our people carry that inheritance forward. Their expertise turns lessons from one country into possibilities for another. Their commitment turns those possibilities into progress.

They are the strength of this institution—and the reason we can ask more of its future.

Today, the challenge arrives as arithmetic: a gap of roughly 800 million jobs. Behind that number is a young woman with a degree and no employer. A young man with a trade and no electricity. A generation asking: is there a place for me?

A job is not a statistic. A job is dignity.

It is the difference between a young person who can build a future; and a young person awaiting one. Leave that potential unrealized, and the consequences cross border.

Give it opportunity, and the benefits cross borders too. That is why development is an investment in our collective future.

This institution is rising to that challenge.

Not to recreate the development model of the last generation—but to build one equal to the expectations of the next. A model that evolves as countries do.

Public money where markets can't yet reach. Private capital where it can create jobs and scale. Philanthropy to take early risk and unlock new ideas. Technology to make every dollar go further.

And a World Bank Group that brings it together around what each country needs. That is the future of development we are working toward.

The jobs gap is a projection. It does not have to be our future.

We have begun to show what this model can deliver. Now we must give it the scale and pace the next generation demands.

That future is ours to build.

item.title: World Bank Group Launches Philanthropy Hub to Unlock Capital, Knowledge and Networks for Development
item.description: BANGKOK, October 12, 2026 The World Bank Group today launched its Philanthropy Hub, a new platform to deepen collaboration with philanthropic organizations and other partners.
item.content:encoded:
BANGKOK, October 12, 2026 - The World Bank Group today launched its Philanthropy Hub, a new platform to deepen collaboration with philanthropic organizations and other partners.

The Philanthropy Hub is part of a broader World Bank Group effort to make it easier to move from innovative ideas and pilot projects to scaled solutions, and from isolated efforts to collective action. As a single-entry point to the World Bank Group, the Hub will identify the best opportunities for philanthropic capital, solutions, and knowledge. It will also help shape the future of philanthropy for development through knowledge sharing, innovative partnerships, and aligning capital around shared priorities.

The launch comes at a time of rising development needs and constrained public resources. Philanthropic organizations are playing an increasingly active role, bringing not just grant funding but also investment capital, expertise, and the ability to convene partners. This support is already making a difference, with organizations contributing to the World Bank Group initiatives such as Mission 300, Health Works, and Water Forward, with tangible results on the ground.

"As development needs grow and resources come under pressure, partnership matters more than ever. Philanthropic organizations bring deep expertise and innovative solutions that align closely with our core missions and jobs agenda. The Philanthropy Hub will connect ideas, resources and partners to take those solutions to scale, and to deliver for people and communities around the world," Paschal Donohoe, Managing Director and Chief Knowledge Officer, World Bank Group.

The Philanthropy Hub was launched at the first World Bank Group Philanthropy Forumduring the World Bank Group-IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok. Co-convened with Asian Venture Philanthropy Network, the Institute of Philanthropy, the OECD's netFWD, and the Philanthropy Asia Alliance by Temasek Trust, the Forum brought together more than 200 leaders from philanthropic foundations and networks, family offices, development institutions, and partner organizations.

On the sidelines of the Forum, two leading philanthropic networks in Asia signed Memoranda of Understanding with the World Bank Group:

  • Through AVPN’s extensive regional network, foundations, social investors and private-sector partners can join forces to support World Bank Group initiatives. AVPN also announced a dedicated fund to support Health Works, the World Bank Group initiative to help provide 1.5 billion people with access to quality, affordable health services, by financing technical assistance.
  • Temasek Trust’s experience in mobilizing philanthropic capital, convening partners, and advancing innovative financing approaches will help develop scalable partnership models, anchored in World Bank Group priority initiatives such as AgriConnect, Health Works, and Water Forward.

Knowledge is at the heart of the Philanthropy Hub. A growing network of Knowledge Partners will help ensure that research, data, and practical experience translate into real impact in the countries where the World Bank Group works. The network spans organizations with strong regional presence, such as the Mo Ibrahim Foundation, Latimpacto, the Philanthropy Asia Alliance and the Centre for Asian Philanthropy and Society; strategy and advisory partners, including the Boston Consulting Group, Bridgespan, Dalberg, and Coefficient Giving; and academic and research institutions, including the Marshall Institute at London School of Economics and Indiana University’s Lilly Family School of Philanthropy.
